text:
Droit de la famille — 252015

2025 QCCS 4946

SUPERIOR COURT

CANADA

PROVINCE OF QUÉBEC

DISTRICT OF

MONTREAL

No: 500-12-349614-218

On December 11, 2025

______________________________________________________________________

BY THE HONOURABLE LOUIS LACOURSIÈRE,
J.S.C.

______________________________________________________________________

M. V.

Plaintiff

v.

T. M.

Defendant

______________________________________________________________________

JUDGMENT

(Declinatory exception
and Modification of accessory measures)

______________________________________________________________________

[
1
]

The Court is seized of Defendant’s
Demand for declinatory exception and of Plaintiff’s Application to modify
accessory measures and cancel child support and arrears.

I.

Context

[
2
]

The context is the following.

[
3
]

On August 20, 2021, the parties were divorced.
The judgment provided that Defendant, the mother, would have the majority of
parenting time and that Plaintiff, the father, would have access to the
children X, born on [...], 2015 and Y, born on [...], 2011.

[
4
]

The divorce judgment provided that the father
would continue to pay for private school tuition and would pay a total of $ 200
monthly in the Registered Education Savings Plan (RESP) accounts for the
children, without any other child support payable at that time.

[
5
]

The Plaintiff moved to Israel in January 2022.

[
6
]

On October 9, 2024, the Superior Court
authorized the Defendant, on a safeguard order, to register the children in
psychological therapy without Plaintiff’s prior consent and to make decisions
alone regarding the children.

[
7
]

On April 23, 2025, the Superior Court heard an
application from the Defendant to modify accessory measures. Amongst other
orders, the Court:

-

granted the mother full parental time and
custody;

-

granted supervised access to the father, under
amicable agreement with the mother;

-

ordered the payment of child support by the father
of $ 1,281.46 per month, retroactively to January 1, 2025, according to
the federal child support guidelines;

-

determined that the special expenses for the
children would be paid by the mother and father in proportions of 61 % and
39 % respectively; and

-

authorized the mother to relocate to Florida,
U.S.A., with the children.

[the April judgment]

[
8
]

There was no appeal of this judgment, rendered
by default.

[
9
]

On July 14, 2025, the Plaintiff, then
represented by attorney, applied, on a safeguard basis, for access to the
children as he was then in Town A from Israel. He was granted supervised access
on July 21, 2025. The Court noted then that the mother would move to Florida
with the children before the next school year.

[
10
]

In the same application, the father asked the Court, also on a
safeguard order, for a modification of the child support payment from $ 1,281.46
per month to $ 626 less travel fees (from and to Israel) for a monthly
amount of $ 292; he also requested a cancellation of arrears for child
support, which were in the amount of $ 17,805 as of May 31
st
,
2025, and cancellation of child support as of the mother’s relocation to
Florida.

[
11
]

The Court did not grant these requests by way of a safeguard order.

[
12
]

On July 22, 2025, the hearing on the merits was scheduled for
October 28,2025.

[
13
]

Defendant and the children moved to the U.S. on September 25, 2025
[1]
. They have signed a lease
there
[2]
.
There is no doubt that they intend to remain in the U.S.

[
14
]

On October 10, 2025, the Defendant’s attorney notified a Notice of a
declinatory exception, announcing that it would ask the Superior Court to
decline jurisdiction.

[
15
]

The Court heard the arguments both on the declinatory exception and
on the merits of the Application to modify the accessory measures.

[
16
]

It will first deal with the issue of the declinatory exception
considering the recent change of residence of the Defendant and the fact that
both parties are no longer domiciled in Québec.

II.

The Declinatory Exception

[
17
]

Defendant alleges that neither party resides or is domiciled in the
Province of Québec, Plaintiff residing and domiciled in Israel and Defendant
and the minor children now living in Florida.

[
18
]

She states that, as the Plaintiff has desisted from his conclusions
regarding parental time, the Superior Court is deprived of its jurisdiction in
accordance with art. 3142 C.C.Q.

[
19
]

She alleges that, as the remaining conclusions of Plaintiff’s
Application relate to child support, the cancellation of arrears of child
support and the cancellation of child support, the Superior Court should
decline jurisdiction, the jurisdiction of the State of Florida, namely the 17
th

Judicial Circuit of Florida for family law matters, being significantly more
appropriate to resolve the dispute in issue.

[
20
]

The Defendant adds that neither the “Federal Tables” nor the “Québec
Tables” for determination of child support are applicable in the current
circumstances of the parties and that the authority of the State of Florida
would be better placed to determine the current needs of the children.

[
21
]

She argues that, even if the Superior Court had jurisdiction, it
would be limited to the issue of arrears until September 25, 2025, when the
Defendant moved to the U.S., and that, in any event, the Court should apply the
doctrine of
forum non conveniens,
codified at art. 3135 C.C.Q., and decide
that Florida, not Québec, would be the best forum.

[
22
]

The Plaintiff insists that the Superior Court has jurisdiction. He
adds that the declinatory exception was notified late and should be dismissed
for this very reason.

[
23
]

The Court is of the view that it has jurisdiction to decide on the
matters still in issue in Plaintiff’s Application.

[
24
]

Articles 3135, 3142 and 3143 C.C.Q. are relevant and read as
follows:

3135.
Even
though a Québec authority has jurisdiction to hear a dispute, it may,
exceptionally and on an application by a party, decline jurisdiction if it
considers that the authorities of another State are in a better position to
decide the dispute.

[
…
]

3142.
Québec authorities have jurisdiction to decide as to the custody
of a child provided he is domiciled in Québec.

3143.
Québec
authorities have jurisdiction to decide actions in matters of support or
applications for review of a foreign support judgment that may be recognized in
Québec, if one of the parties has his domicile or residence in Québec.

[
25
]

The fact that the Defendant and the children moved to the U.S.
during the proceedings does not deprive the Superior Court of its jurisdiction.
The jurisdiction of the Court is determined according to the domicile of one of
the parties at the time of institution of the proceedings
[3]
.

[
26
]

The Plaintiff has agreed not to proceed on his conclusions with
respect to parental time. However, the Court finds it necessary to address
briefly the issue of custody.

[
27
]

It is generally accepted that Québec courts no longer have
jurisdiction over the child once they authorize the custodial parent to
relocate abroad with the child and to establish a new residence, that such
authorization has become a final judgment and that the custodial parent has
moved
[4]
.

[
28
]

On April 23, 2025, the Superior Court authorized the Defendant to
relocate to the U.S.A., with the children.

[
29
]

On September 25, 2025, the Defendant relocated to Florida with the
children. The Québec court therefore ceases to have jurisdiction over them from
that date onward regarding the exercise of parental time.

[
30
]

However, the Plaintiff still seeks two general
orders, one regarding the exercise of parental
authority, children’s health, education, religion and so forth and the other
regarding consultation between the parties on decisions regarding the children.

[
31
]

Does the Court retain jurisdiction over the remaining attributes of
parental authority? The Court believes that jurisdiction in this matter should
follow the solution adopted with respect to child support.

[
32
]

In accordance with the guidance of the Court of Appeal
[5]
, there is no doubt that, in
matters of child support, the Superior Court retained jurisdiction despite the
Defendant’s relocation to Florida with the children.

[
33
]

The Superior Court has been seized of the matter involving the
parties since February 2021 and Canadian and Québec law has been applied since.

[
34
]

The Plaintiff instituted his recourse in the Superior Court in July
of 2025 for sound reasons. Not only was he seeking changes to the April
judgment rendered by this Court earlier in the year but he was also looking for
safeguard orders to cancel arrears for child support.

[
35
]

However, the Defendant argues that, even if the Superior Court
retained jurisdiction, it would only cover arrears up to September 25, 2025,
when the Defendant moved to the U.S. She also states that, in any case, the
Court should apply the doctrine of
forum non conveniens
under article
3135 C.C.Q. and find Florida to be the more appropriate forum.

[
36
]

The Court agrees with this last proposition.

[
37
]

Once the jurisdiction of the Superior Court is established, as is
the case here, recourse to art. 3135 C.C.Q. is exceptional. The article itself
states so. The caselaw illustrates this
[6]
.

[
38
]

After globally weighing the factors identified
by the Québec Court of Appeal in
Droit de la famille – 131294
[7]

to
determine whether another court is clearly better suited, the Court is of the
view that the Defendant’s Motion should be partly granted and that the Florida
court is the appropriate forum for the period following her relocation to
Florida with the children. The following reasons are very significant to make
this matter an exceptional one:

a.

articles 33
and
34
of the
Québec Civil Code
require that decisions
affecting a child prioritize the child’s best interests and rights, and that
the child be heard when age and discernment allow;

b.

although the Court currently has no jurisdiction in the matter of
child custody but still retains jurisdiction regarding the child support, the
17
th
Judicial Circuit of Florida for family law matters is now in a
better position to determine the personal and material needs of the children
who now are residing and are domiciled in Town B, Florida;

c.

neither the Federal nor the Québec guidelines are now appropriate to
the current situation of the children;

d.

witnesses living in the State of Florida may be called upon to
testify with regards to the children's needs;

e.

the limited financial means of Defendant who, since April 2024, has
not received from Plaintiff any alimentary support for the children; and

f.

there is no meaningful connection to Québec, as neither the parties
nor, obviously, the minor children, reside or are domiciled there.

[
39
]

The Court therefore declines jurisdiction to cancel child support
after September 25, 2025, and to grant any order regarding the exercise of
parental authority, as the Florida court is better positioned to decide.

[
40
]

The Court will now deal with the Plaintiff’s Application to modify
accessory measures and cancel arrears.

III.

The Application to modify accessory measures

[
41
]

Excluding issues of parenting time, the conclusions initially sought
by the Plaintiff on July 14, 2025 are the following:

ORDER          monthly child support in the
amount of 292 $ retroactively as of                                  January
1
st
, 2025;

CANCEL         arrears in child support owed
by the Plaintiff to Revenu Québec in the              amount of
$ 17 805,30;

TAKE ACT      of
Applicant’s offer to pay for tuition retroactively in the amount of $ 3 798;

CANCEL         child
support as of October 1, 2025 following the Defendant’s relocation to Florida;

ORDER          that
the parties share the exercise of their parental authority with respect to the
minor children and that they shall decide together all major matters relating
to their health, education, religion, residence, domicile, and welfare, while
taking into consideration their best interest;

ORDER          that
the parties agree to consult one other in advance and in writing with respect
to significant decisions to be made regarding the minor child’s health,
education, religion, residence, domicile and welfare;

[
42
]

The Plaintiff’s July 14 Application was amended at the very
beginning of the October 28 hearing. The conclusions sought on the arrears and
the child support became as follows, all other conclusions remaining the same:

AMEND          arrears
on child support owed by the Plaintiff to Revenu Québec to $ 3,638.32 in
child support arrears and $ 3,798 in tuition arrears;

CANCEL         child
support as of October 1, 2025 following the Defendant’s relocation to Florida.

[
43
]

The amount of child support arrears as modified by Plaintiff is
based on the child support that Plaintiff now alleges he should have paid, i.e.
$ 454,92 monthly, rather than $ 1,281.46 monthly.

•

The April judgment

[
44
]

It is worth stating, from the outset, that the Defendant’s application
which was decided by the April judgment was served upon Plaintiff by e-mail and
that the latter did not respond nor reply in any way.

[
45
]

There was no appeal of the April judgment.

[
46
]

The Plaintiff acknowledged at the hearing receiving the proceedings
leading to the April judgment but testified that it was sent to him while he
was in mourning after his mother’s passing. He therefore ignored said
proceedings.

[
47
]

As to the April judgment itself, Plaintiff said it was received in
his SPAM mail; he states that, when he opened it, on the 14
th
of
May, the delay to appeal was “almost expired”. He mentioned that he could not
appeal, even if he had time left to do it, notably because his lawyer was going
on vacation.

[
48
]

These explanations are clear but not at all convincing. They rather
lead the Court to conclude that the Plaintiff seemed not to realize the relevancy
of the court proceedings, which is rather difficult to understand as they concern
the fate of Plaintiff’s family for months and years to come.

[
49
]

The Court has no ground at all to find that the April judgment
should not be binding on the Plaintiff.

•

The obligations under the divorce judgment

[
50
]

The Court will now deal briefly with Plaintiff’s obligations as per
the divorce judgment.

[
51
]

The divorce judgment provided for child support in the form of
Plaintiff paying for the private school tuition of the children and
contributing to their RESP.

[
52
]

At the time of the divorce, August 20, 2021, the private Jewish
School ([School A]) charged $ 431 monthly in tuition, the parties benefiting
from a “tuition break”. The monthly contribution of the Plaintiff to the RESP
account was to be $ 200.

[
53
]

There was no other child support payable as per the divorce
judgment.

[
54
]

The April judgment ruled,
inter alia
, that as of April 23,
2025, the Plaintiff owed the following amount:

-

$ 350

for the school
tuition for June 2024;

-

$ 3,448

for the school
tuition for 2024/2025;

-

$ 7,600

for RESP;

$ 11,398

Total amount

[
55
]

The Plaintiff mentioned that he had a verbal agreement with
Defendant that he would stop paying the monthly amount of $ 200 for the
RESP as of when he moved to Israel, in 2022. He said that the fact that
Defendant waited many months to claim the RESP amounts from him is evidence of
the existence of this agreement. He acknowledged, however, that he should have
put this “agreement” in writing.

[
56
]

For her part, Defendant stated that she only found out in or around
September 2024 that the RESP contribution was not being paid by the Plaintiff
because it is only at that time that the Plaintiff’s sister, who was managing
the account, gave her access to the account.

[
57
]

In the absence of persuasive evidence of the existence of an
agreement to cancel the Plaintiff’s obligation with regards to the $ 200
monthly payment in the RESP account, the Court does not accept the Plaintiff’s
argument that this obligation was in any way modified by agreement with the
Defendant.

•

The child support as per the April
judgment

[
58
]

The April judgment established child support payable by the
Plaintiff. It was set at $ 1,281.46 monthly, as per the “applicable federal
child support guidelines”, as of January 1, 2025.

[
59
]

In looking into the court records, it appears that the monthly child
support obligation arrived at in the April judgment was based partly on a Child
support determination form signed by the Defendant on April 23, 2025 which
included net special expenses of some $ 18,771, including private school
and therapy for the children, based on a total income for her of $ 55,460
and for Plaintiff of $ 40,000
[8]
.
The amount of $ 1,281.46 in monthly child support was arrived at by using these
numbers
[9]
.

[
60
]

With a yearly income of $ 40,000 for the Plaintiff, the basic
amount of monthly child support for both children was $ 626 as per the
Federal
child support guidelines
. To this amount was added the Plaintiff’s share of the
annual special expenses then claimed by the Defendant
[10]
, $ 18,771 for the year. His
share of the yearly special expenses was set at $ 7,865.49 or
$ 655.46 monthly, for a total amount of monthly child support of
$ 1,281.46.

[
61
]

Justice Edwards obviously took the amount of special expenses at
face value, which is not surprising in the circumstances.

•

Modification of child support and arrears

[
62
]

Does the evidence adduced warrant the conclusions sought by the
Plaintiff to reduce the amount of child support payable by him from January 1,
2025 until September 25, 2025 and to modify child support arrears from January
1, 2025 to September 25, 2025?

[
63
]

The Plaintiff claims that he had always paid child support,
excluding the RESP payments, and that an event which occurred in April 2024,
during a visit that he made from Israel to Town A, exacerbated the situation
between the parties and created a situation where Y, always so close to her
dad, refused to talk to him.

[
64
]

The situation was serious enough to lead to recommendations that the
children attend therapy, which was eventually authorized by the Court on
October 9, 2024.

[
65
]

The situation also led to the Plaintiff having difficulties seeing
his children upon his visits in Town A. Out of anger, by his own admission, the
Plaintiff stopped paying child support. The Plaintiff now acknowledges that
this was a mistake.

[
66
]

He adds, however, that he had contributed to his children’s support
in other ways. In December 2023, he paid around $ 3,000 towards Y’s
Bat Mitzvah and also paid $ 7,119 towards her four-week 2024 overnight
camp in Ontario
[11]
.
He also opened for Y an investment account in which he deposited $ 1,300.

[
67
]

Defendant stated that she knew nothing about this account; she did
acknowledge, however, that the Plaintiff paid for Ys’s camp.

[
68
]

When asked why he decided to make a contribution to his daughter in
an investment account rather than pay the child support, Plaintiff replied that
there was an agreement between Defendant and him that the child support did not
have to be paid and that he was free to contribute for his daughter as he
wished.

[
69
]

There is no conclusive evidence of the existence of such an
agreement.

[
70
]

Moreover, the facts raised by the Plaintiff to amend and reduce the
arrears he owes, such as expenses for summer camp and various cash allowances
for the children, all took place prior to the April judgment.

[
71
]

The Plaintiff describes a difficult personal situation as ground for
his Application.

[
72
]

He states that he owes $ 64,000, as appears from his Schedule I
form signed on October 27, 2025 and filed on the morning of the hearing. He
owes Revenu Québec $ 21,000, his dad $ 12,500 and has bank and credit
card debts for the balance. In fact, as of September 5, 2025, the Plaintiff
owed Revenu Québec an amount of $ 24,339.12
[12]
.

[
73
]

The Plaintiff has been working for a construction company in Israel.
He started on February 17, 2023. His job was to order stocks and equipment for
the construction sites. He describes this as a very stressful job.

[
74
]

He said that the difficulty he had seeing his children in July of
2025 put a lot of strain on him. As mentioned before, his visits with X were supervised
by his father or his sister and such visits were, in his view, made very difficult
by the Defendant.

[
75
]

He returned to Israel on the 11
th
of August 2025. He said
that he was shocked to get a note, about a week later, from his son that the
latter did not want to talk to him anymore. This came as a surprise to him after
a visit where he felt he had bonded very well with his son. The Plaintiff is
convinced that X’s refusal to talk to him is the Defendant’s doing.

[
76
]

The Plaintiff said that, in the aftermath of this, he fell into a
depression, did not show up at work for a month and lost his job. He mentioned
that he has no medical certificate relating to his depression. He said that he
did not want to consult a doctor because he is seeking to obtain a gun licence,
as he lives in a dangerous area of Israel, close to the Gaza border, and that
such a medical record would hurt his chances to obtain his licence.

[
77
]

The Plaintiff’s employment was therefore terminated on October 1,
2025
[13]
,
but he did not work, nor did he receive any pay, in the month of September.

[
78
]

The Plaintiff was paid 15,000 shekels monthly
[14]
, which comes up to approximately
$ 6,374.47
[15]
.
His salary was higher in July because of bonuses paid by the employer for that
month, and lower in August, $ 3,483.34.

[
79
]

Defendant’s attorney suggested that the proper amount to be used to
determine the yearly income of the Plaintiff for 2025 is the year-to-date
taxable income of the Plaintiff as of August 2025, i.e.  149,959 shekels
[16]
. This amount, for a year, is
224,938 shekels, or $ 96,723
[17]
.

[
80
]

The Plaintiff’s attorney suggested for her part an estimated income
of $ 50,348.09
[18]

as this amount takes into account the fact that the Plaintiff no longer has a
job and has received no income since September 1, 2025.

*.*.*

[
81
]

The Plaintiff did not remember his 2024 income. He stated that he
earned 8,500 shekels a month in 2023. He never supplied the Defendant with
proofs of income in 2023 or 2024.

[
82
]

Plaintiff sold his house in Town A in 2019
[19]
after the parties separated.
He was asked how much money he received from the sale. His answer: “one hundred
something thousand” dollars. When asked to be more precise, he said maybe
$ 110,000 or $ 120,000. When asked what he did with the money, he
said he would not answer that, that it was “none of your business”, calling the
exercise “harassment”.

[
83
]

On August 10, 2025, at Duty Free Town A, the Plaintiff bought
perfume for $ 505 as a gift for his girlfriend. When asked how he was able
to pay that and not able to find money to support his children, he did not
answer the question. He added that the Defendant received Canada and Québec
government money to support the children and that he did not receive any such
money.

[
84
]

These answers show little, if any, will from the Plaintiff to allow
the Court to find out the truth. It is obvious that the Plaintiff is furious at
Defendant for, in his opinion, turning his children against him. It is also
obvious that the Plaintiff did not understand the purpose of the court hearing,
notably finding the truth about his income, as he continually answered that
legitimate questions about his spending were intrusions into his personal life.

[
85
]

The Plaintiff says that he is currently living in a house owned by a
charity organisation because he has no money and no job
[20]
. He said that he lived with
his girlfriend until the end of August.

[
86
]

He stated that the money he saved from his job went to pay for his
travelling to Canada. He paid $ 2,191.38 USD for his return trip from Town
C to Town A from July 13 to August 11, 2025
[21]
.
He is not counting on spending any more money for travelling to see his
children because he knows that Defendant will not welcome him to Florida.

[
87
]

The Defendant, for her part, lost her job in the fall of 2024.

[
88
]

She denies having “turned” the children against their dad. She
stated that the Plaintiff asked X in June 2025 to go to Israel and that he did
not agree, notably because the country was at war. X was also disturbed when he
found out that his dad had a girlfriend.

[
89
]

The Defendant does not believe that Plaintiff is not working but it
is difficult for her, as he lives in Israel, to verify the Plaintiff’s income
and whereabouts.

*.*.*

[
90
]

The Court has some sympathy for the Plaintiff, who misses his
children and states that he is heartbroken for being so estranged from them.

[
91
]

This being said, the Plaintiff did little to convince the Court that
the situation as it stands should be substantially modified.

[
92
]

The Plaintiff is basically asking the Court to revise the April judgment
based on what could have been argued by him in April of 2025. This Court is not
sitting in appeal of the April judgment.

[
93
]

The Plaintiff is arguing that, as far as tuition payments are
concerned, he owes and is willing to pay $ 3,448 for the whole academic year
2024-2025 and $ 350 for June 2024 for a total of $ 3,798, which are
exactly the amounts mentioned in the April judgment. He states that any money
claimed to have been paid by the Defendant for tuition for 2024- 2025, i.e.
$ 15,043, has not been paid by her
[22]
.
There is no clear evidence of that, as Defendant says that she paid this whole
amount by herself. In any event, this evidence should have been adduced by the
Plaintiff before Justice Edwards.

[
94
]

The Plaintiff also asks that his child support be fixed at
$ 454.92 based on a $ 50,348 annual income i.e. $ 788.25
monthly, as per the
Federal child support guidelines
less an amount of
$ 333.33 monthly, or $ 4,000 yearly, for travel fees to see his
children for a total monthly amount of $ 454,92. This is based on the real
income of the Plaintiff as per the evidence he provided
[23]
.

[
95
]

The Plaintiff asks that the child support be suspended as of
September 1, 2025, rather than October 1, 2025 as initially asked in the
amendment made on the morning of the hearing, because the Plaintiff had no
income in September of 2025.

[
96
]

The Defendant has a totally different position. She states that the
Plaintiff was very fortunate that the April judgment used a $ 40,000
yearly income for him for purposes of establishing the child support, when he
was in fact earning a lot more.

[
97
]

She states that the Court has no reason to rule on any arrears
which predate the April judgment, liquidated at $ 11,398.

[
98
]

The Court agrees with this last argument.

[
99
]

The April judgment is a final judgment and the Court will not deal
with evidence which predates the April judgment and was used to render said
judgment.

[
100
]

What are the changes since the April judgment?

[
101
]

The Plaintiff’s annual income is higher than $ 40,000. There is
no longer private school fees, nor therapy fees which, in the understanding of
the Court, made up a lot of the special expenses of $ 18,771 claimed by
Defendant on April 23, 2025.

[
102
]

As stated above, to determine the Plaintiff’s income, Defendant used
the August 2025 paystub
[24]

of the Plaintiff which showed a year-to-date income of $ 149,959 shekels.
Converted into dollars, with the October 28, 2025 conversion rate, the amount
is $ 96,245 for the full year. This is the income that the Defendant
suggests should be used to determine child support.

[
103
]

The amount of child support for 2025 as per the federal table should
therefore have been, in the Defendant’s view, $ 1,352 monthly.

[
104
]

The Defendant’s position does not take into account that the
Plaintiff lost his job and had no income as of September 2025 because she does
not believe he lost his job, nor does she believe that the Plaintiff’s
testimony and evidence are reliable.

[
105
]

Even though the Plaintiff’s credibility was lacking on many fronts,
there is a termination letter in the file which tips the scale in favour of the
Plaintiff’s version that he lost his job. There is also evidence that he is now
living in a shelter and that he has many debts. Did he lose his job because of
his own fault? There is not enough in the evidence to suggest this.

[
106
]

For the sake determining a new amount of child support, the Court
will therefore use the income as of August 31, 2025 determined by the
Plaintiff, i.e. $ 50,348. It will make the new child support obligation of the
Plaintiff retroactive to July 15, 2025, date of service of the Application.

[

]

The amount of child support will therefore be $ 788 monthly.
However, the Court will not deduct any amount for travel fees. First of all,
the Plaintiff moved first, away from his family, in 2022. Secondly, and more
important, he has stated clearly that he would not go to Florida to visit his
children, at least in the foreseeable future.
